title: His own gambling club and the mostly white crowds on State Street
summary: Compton ran a club with gambling tables, cleared with Colosimo; the crowds were 70-75 percent white and there were no raids.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Now, I had a club here in 41 and just, you're walking, just like walking in an ordinary tavern. And my first table was blackjack. The next table was the walled-in and rubber-lined dice table. An old pool, it had been an old pool table and you had those sides put on it and lined with rubber. Oh yeah. And then a poker table. And I had to, or Big Jim Colosimo, I had to go down to see Colosimo. And I was okayed. I was okayed for those people.
Most of the customers, were they colored or white in those clubs along State Street?

More about, oh, I'd say 70 or 75 percent white. At the E-Light and Dreamland and those places. Yeah. We'd get the white crowds around 12 or 1 o'clock every night. See, the E-Light and Dreamland had balcony all the way around. And the whites, a lot of, every night we'd get a bunch of, about 20 or 30 or more white fellas with tuxedos on. So naturally we knew there were musicians coming from that yard around 1 or 1.30. Was there dancing at most of those places or mostly just drinking or what? Yeah. Dancing and drinking and they usually had a couple of entertainers. Girls. Nettie and Caroline and the James sisters. Nettie could name them better than I could.
Nettie and Caroline and the James sisters. Nettie and Caroline and the James sisters. Did you have any trouble with the Prohibition raids in those days? No, no, no, no.
Never started, never, never was in a raid the whole time I played in those places.
And that was after Prohibition too?
Yes. Did they sell? No, before Prohibition. Before Prohibition too? Yeah. Because I went to the E-Light 1910.
